unit.title: Analyse and interpret workforce development trends

summary: This unit teaches you to study how the workforce is changing and to turn what you find into plans for developing people. You will learn to find and judge sources of labour market information, work out growth rates, turnover, shares and moving averages, spot trends such as an ageing workforce, migration, automation and remote working, avoid false conclusions, and present findings that lead to training and recruitment decisions.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you, as a manager or senior supervisor, to find out **how the workforce is changing** (who is working, in which jobs, with which skills) and to decide what your organisation should do about it. Workforce development means planning how people are recruited, trained, kept and moved on so that the organisation has the skills it needs.

Every organisation in Jamaica, from a hotel group in Montego Bay to a parish health department or a Kingston call centre, depends on having enough people with the right skills at the right time. Managers who study the trends early can train, recruit and plan ahead. Managers who do not find themselves short of skilled staff with no time to fix it.
**Who it is for:** supervisors and managers who plan staffing, training or careers, or who must report on workforce matters to senior management.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Explain workforce trends
Say what a trend is, and separate it from seasonal patterns and one-off events.
Find and judge information
Use internal and external sources, such as staff records, STATIN labour force data and industry reports, and check how reliable each one is.
Work out the numbers
Calculate percentage change, shares, turnover, unemployment and participation rates, moving averages and simple projections, and check every sum twice.
Identify the main trends
Recognise ageing, migration of skilled workers, automation, remote and hybrid work, the gig economy, skills shortages and the demand for qualifications.
Interpret with care
Avoid false causes, weak samples and over-confident forecasts; use PESTLE and scenarios.
Link trends to plans
Show what each trend means for recruitment, training, retention and the organisation's strategic plan.
Report and present
Present findings clearly, protect personal data and recommend actions that decision makers can approve.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios and calculations.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms and quick sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: analysing a made-up workforce data set and presenting charts and an interpretation; and researching an industry's labour market trends and writing a briefing. Each member has a named role and explains their part to the assessor.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, with the base (the number you divide by) written down. Many marks are lost by using the wrong base.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What workforce trends are and why they matter

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Workforce development
Planned action to build the skills and numbers of people an organisation needs
A hotel pays for housekeepers to complete a supervisory course
Trend
A long-term direction of change in data over several periods
The number of staff aged 55 and over rises every year for five years
Seasonal pattern
A change that repeats at the same time each year
More hotel staff are needed from December to April
One-off event
A single event that distorts the figures and should not be projected forward
A hurricane closes a hotel for six weeks
Labour force
All people of working age who are employed, plus those who are unemployed and actively looking for work
Employed 560,000 + unemployed 40,000 = labour force 600,000
Participation rate
Labour force as a percentage of the working-age population
A labour force of 600,000 out of 850,000 working-age people is 70.6%
Unemployment rate
Unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force
Skills gap
The difference between the skills your staff have now and the skills the organisation needs
Staff cannot use the new accounting software
Skills shortage
Employers cannot find enough qualified people in the labour market, even when they try
Few qualified refrigeration technicians are available to hire

blocks.note: A skills gap is **inside** your organisation (you can train to close it). A skills shortage is **in the labour market** (training must happen outside too, or you must change your offer to attract people).
blocks.label: Remember

ul: To **plan ahead**: training takes months or years, so you must start before the need is urgent.
To **spend wisely**: money goes to the skills that will matter, not those that are fading.
To **keep people**: you learn why people leave and what they want from work.
To **support strategy**: the organisation's plan to grow, change or enter new markets needs the people to carry it out.
To **manage risk**: ageing staff, migration and new technology can threaten service if nobody is watching.

blocks.p: Before you project anything, decide which kind of change you are looking at. A **trend** can be projected (with care). A **seasonal pattern** should be planned for each year but not mistaken for growth: a December rise in hotel staff is not a sign that the hotel is growing. A **one-off event** should be noted and then set aside, or the forecast will be wrong.

blocks.note: When you compare two periods, compare like with like: this January with last January, not this January with last October.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: PESTLE: a checklist of outside influences

head: Heading
Workforce examples
rows: Political
Government training policy, youth programmes, public sector reform
Economic
Growth of tourism or business process outsourcing (BPO), inflation, the exchange rate, wage levels
Social
Ageing population, more women in management, young workers who want flexible hours
Technological
Automation, cloud systems, artificial intelligence, mobile payments
Legal
Employment law, occupational safety and health rules, the data protection law, qualification requirements
Environmental
Hurricanes and flooding that close workplaces, drought, the move to green energy jobs

blocks.p: Good analysis starts with good information. Use **more than one source**, so that each one can confirm or challenge the others.

head: Type
Examples
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Internal
Payroll and HR records, staff ages and length of service, training records, exit interviews, absence records, vacancy and recruitment data
Your own organisation's exact position
Gaps, errors and records kept in different ways by different branches
External: national

STATIN Labour Force Survey (employment and unemployment), the Planning Institute of Jamaica's Economic and Social Survey Jamaica (ESSJ), ministry reports, HEART/NSTA Trust training and certification data
National and sector trends
Figures may be a year or more old
External: industry
Industry association surveys, sector skills studies, job advertisements, trade journals
Skills demand in your sector
May reflect one group's interests
External: other
Reports by researchers and international bodies, news items, social media polls
Context and ideas
Method and sample may be weak or unknown

blocks.p: **Primary data** is information you collect yourself, for example a staff survey. **Secondary data** is information someone else collected for another purpose, such as a national survey, which you then use in your own analysis. Secondary data is cheaper and wider, but you must check that it fits your question.
Ask these questions of every source and write the answers in a source table.

head: Question
Why it matters
rows: Who produced it, and why?
An independent statistics office is more neutral than a seller of equipment or a lobby group.
When was it produced?
A labour market in constant change makes old figures misleading.
How was it produced?
A random survey of thousands of people is stronger than a poll of 25 friends.
How big and how representative is the sample?
A small or self-selected sample may not speak for everyone.
Is it consistent with other sources?
If three sources agree, you can trust the trend more.
Does it fit our question?
National data may hide the position in one parish or one industry.

blocks.note: A claim such as "half of all jobs will disappear" is not evidence. Look for the method, the date, who paid for it, and whether similar organisations have seen the same results.
blocks.label: Remember

ol: Check for missing values and obvious errors (for example an age of 150).
Check that totals add up and that branches use the same definitions (for example "leaver").
Mark any gaps and say how you handled them (left out, estimated or queried with the source).
Keep the original file unchanged and work on a copy.

blocks.p: Workforce data includes personal details. The data protection law in Jamaica sets general rules: collect only what you need, use it only for its stated purpose, keep it secure and limit who can see it. In a trends report, **use totals, groups and percentages, not names**. Remove names and identifying details from exit interview comments before they are shared, and store the files where only authorised people can open them.

blocks.note: Source reliability, such as STATIN's labour force surveys and the PIOJ's ESSJ, should still be checked for date and definitions. A good source can still be old or wrong for your question.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Main workforce trends and what they mean

blocks.p: The trends below affect many Jamaican employers. For each one, a manager must be able to say what it is, how to see it in the data and what to do about it.

head: Trend
What to look for in the data
Likely implication for workforce development
rows: Ageing workforce and retirement
A rising average age; a large share of staff aged 55 and over; few young people in key trades
Succession planning, mentoring, apprenticeships, recording expert know-how, phased retirement
Migration of skilled workers (often called brain drain)
Nurses, teachers, technicians or IT staff leaving for jobs overseas; exit interviews citing pay abroad
Review pay and career paths, offer training that is valued, train extra people, build a pipeline
Automation and digital technology
Routine tasks (data entry, simple clerical work) falling; new roles in data, systems and support
Reskilling and upskilling; new job descriptions; training before the system arrives
Growth of BPO and services
More call centres and back-office firms in Kingston, Portmore and Montego Bay; many adverts for service and IT skills
Customer service, communication, languages and IT training; co-operation with training providers
Gig and freelance work
More young people earning from short online jobs for overseas clients rather than one employer
Flexible contracts, skills for freelancers, competition for talent
Remote and hybrid working
Staff splitting the week between home and office
Training supervisors to lead and support staff at a distance, clear digital tools and rules
Qualification and certification
More adverts asking for NVQ-J, CAPE or degrees
Support staff to be assessed and certified; use certification as evidence of skills
Youth unemployment alongside skills shortages
Many young job seekers but employers say few are job-ready
Placements, internships, links with schools and HEART/NSTA Trust
Seasonal demand (tourism)
Peaks and troughs in staff each year
Flexible staffing plans, cross-training, planned recruitment before each season

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Upskilling
Training staff to do their current job better or with new tools
Accounts clerks learn the new features of the accounting software
Reskilling
Training staff for a different role
A data entry clerk becomes a customer data analyst
Apprenticeship
Paid training with an employer, combined with study, leading to a recognised trade qualification
A trainee electrician working under a certified electrician
Succession planning
Preparing people to take over key roles when the present holders leave
A deputy plant manager is trained to become plant manager

blocks.note: HEART/NSTA Trust offers training and NVQ-J assessment and certification across many occupations. Employers can use it to train new entrants and to certify staff who already have the skills but no paper to show it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Name the trend and show the evidence
Estimate how many people and which jobs are affected
Say when it will matter (this year, in three years, in ten)
Choose responses: train, recruit, redeploy, retain or change the work
Set measures such as turnover or time to fill a vacancy
Review the figures regularly and adjust

blocks.p: Level 5 managers are expected to calculate and check the main workforce measures. **Write the formula, show the working and check the answer.** Always say what the base is.

head: Measure
Formula
Worked example
rows: Percentage change
(new − old) ÷ old × 100
Staff from 240 to 264: 24 ÷ 240 × 100 = 10% increase
Share (percentage of the whole)
part ÷ whole × 100
36 of 240 staff are under 25: 36 ÷ 240 × 100 = 15%
Staff turnover rate
leavers ÷ average number of staff × 100
18 leavers, average 120 staff: 18 ÷ 120 × 100 = 15%
Unemployment rate
unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
Participation rate
labour force ÷ working-age population × 100
Moving average
add the last few values, divide by how many
Compound growth
start × (1 + rate) for each year
Workforce gap
staff needed − staff available
Need 45, can train 27 from within: recruit 18

blocks.note: Some organisations measure turnover against the opening headcount instead of the average. Use the method your organisation states, say which you used, and use the same method every year so that years can be compared.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A hotel in Negril had 200 staff in 2023, 210 in 2024 and 231 in 2025. Leavers were 30, 28 and 33.

ul: Turnover 2024: 28 ÷ 210 × 100 = **13.3%** (using that year's staff number as the base).
Meaning: staff numbers are rising faster, but turnover is rising too. The hotel is growing and also losing a higher share of staff, so it must look at why people leave.

blocks.p: Check: 10% of 210 is 21, and 210 + 21 = 231, so the growth is right. 14.3% of 231 is about 33, so the turnover is right.

A **moving average** smooths out ups and downs so that you can see the direction. Vacancies of 24, 30, 27 and 33 over four months give three-month moving averages of 27 (24, 30, 27) and 30 (30, 27, 33).

A **projection** (or extrapolation) extends a past trend into the future. It assumes that the conditions that caused the trend continue. It is a useful first estimate, but it is only as good as that assumption. Always give a range or scenarios.

head: Purpose
Best chart
rows: Change over time (trainees each year for ten years)
Line graph
Comparing amounts between groups (staff by department)
Bar or column chart
The parts of a whole (share of staff by age band)
Pie chart or stacked bar, if there are few groups
Exact figures for reference
Table

blocks.p: Give every chart a **title that says what it shows**, label the axes and units and name the source.

sections.title: Interpreting the data without being misled

blocks.p: Two measures that tend to move together are **correlated**. That does **not** prove that one causes the other. A third factor may cause both, or the link may be chance. If branches with more training hours also have lower turnover, training may help, but those branches may also have better managers or better pay.

blocks.note: Safe wording: "The two are linked. Before we say training reduces turnover, we should check other causes."
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A **sample** should be large enough and chosen to represent everyone you want to describe.
A survey where only volunteers answer, or where only head office staff respond, can be **biased**.
Eight answers from 600 staff cannot be relied upon.
Ask the same questions of all groups, and follow up non-responders if you can.
Conditions change: demand, laws, technology and the exchange rate.
Rapid growth rarely continues at the same rate for long.
One-off events are mistaken for trends.
Data may be old or incomplete.

blocks.p: When the future is uncertain, prepare plans for **several possible scenarios** rather than one forecast. For a new development that might bring few or many jobs, plan a low, a medium and a high case. For each, decide what you would do, what would signal that the scenario is happening, and when you would decide.

head: Scenario
Staff needed in three years
Response
rows: Low growth
10% more than now
Train existing staff; no extra recruitment
Expected growth
25% more
Train and recruit steadily; link with HEART/NSTA Trust
High growth
50% more
Early recruitment drive, partnership with training providers, temporary staff as a bridge

blocks.note: The figures above are examples of method, not forecasts for any real organisation.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Before you finalise a report, discuss the draft with **line managers**. They see daily work and can tell you whether your findings match what they see. They may also explain odd figures. Use more than one source so that a trend is confirmed, not guessed.
Review trends **regularly** (at least yearly), because conditions change and plans must keep up.

sections.title: Turning analysis into action and reporting it

flow: Link the trend to the organisation's strategic plan and goals
Estimate the skills and numbers needed, now and in one, three and five years
Compare with the skills and numbers you have now (the gap)
Decide how to close each gap: train, recruit, redeploy, partner, change the work
Set targets, budget, owners and dates

blocks.p: Analysis that is not linked to the strategic plan can lead to training nobody needs. If the plan says the firm will open a refrigerated distribution service, the people plan must include refrigeration and cold-chain handling skills.

head: Gap
Options
rows: Skills gap inside the organisation
Training, coaching, mentoring, job rotation, qualifications
Shortage in the labour market
Apprenticeships, links with schools and HEART/NSTA Trust, better pay and conditions, changing the job
Too many staff for a declining task
Redeploy and reskill; manage reductions in line with employment law and consultation
Leaving of experienced staff
Capture know-how in procedures, mentoring, flexible retirement, career paths

head: Part
Content
rows: Summary
The main findings and the decisions needed, in a few lines
Method and sources
What data you used, its dates, and how reliable it is
Findings
Clear charts and tables with headings that say what they show
Implications
What each trend means for recruitment, training and retention
Recommendations
Actions, costs, owners and dates, in order of priority
Limits and next review
What you could not be sure of, and when the analysis will be updated

blocks.note: For a board or senior management team, give a short summary, clear charts and the implications. Lead with what you want them to decide.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Open with the headline finding in one sentence.
Show no more than one idea per chart.
Give the figure and what it means ("15% of technicians may retire within five years, so we need to start training successors now").
End with the decision you need and the cost of waiting.

c1.title: The works department of a municipal corporation
c1.text: Marlon Brown manages the works department of a municipal corporation in Clarendon. It has 60 technicians. Nine of them are aged 55 or older, and 21 are under 30. Over the last year, 5 technicians left (3 retired and 2 resigned). Some of the older technicians are the only people who know how to repair the old water pumps.

c2.title: A business process outsourcing centre in Portmore
c2.text: Keisha Reid is HR manager at a BPO centre in Portmore. It started this year with 800 staff and has grown by 5% a year for the last three years. Monthly vacancies over the last four months were 24, 30, 27 and 33. Of the last 40 job adverts placed by similar centres, 14 asked for Spanish-language skills.

c3.title: Staffing at an Ocho Rios hotel
c3.text: Andrea Williams, the training manager of a hotel in Ocho Rios, is writing a workforce report. The hotel needs about 30% more staff from December to April each year. Over three years, 30 chefs and front-office staff have left. In their exit interviews, 18 of the 30 said they were leaving for better pay overseas. A hurricane in the second year closed the hotel for five weeks.

c4.title: Sources for an insurance company's training plan
c4.text: Delroy Francis is training manager at an insurance company in Kingston. His assistant sends him a WhatsApp poll of 25 of her friends, which says that 80% of recent graduates plan to leave Jamaica. She also brings a brochure from an equipment seller that says half of all office jobs will disappear in five years, and a table of employment by industry from the Economic and Social Survey Jamaica. Delroy also notices that branches with more overtime also have more sick leave.

c5.title: Automation at a Kingston logistics firm
c5.text: A Kingston logistics firm will introduce automated sorting in its warehouse over three years. Forty pickers' jobs will be reduced, and 10 new jobs will be created for system operators and maintenance technicians. Its strategic plan says it will start a refrigerated delivery service. Its largest customer's contract may or may not be renewed next year, so volumes could be much higher or lower.

questions.q: What share of the department's technicians is aged 55 or older?
questions.why: Share = part ÷ whole × 100 = 9 ÷ 60 × 100 = 15%. The base is all 60 technicians. Check: 15% of 60 = 9.

questions.q: What was the department's staff turnover rate for the year, using 60 as the average number of staff?
questions.why: Turnover = leavers ÷ average staff × 100 = 5 ÷ 60 × 100 = 8.3%. Check: 8.3% of 60 is about 5. Retirements count as leavers.

questions.q: Marlon wants to know what skills the department could lose. What should he do first?
o: Advertise for nine new technicians now, before any skills are mapped
Map each older technician's skills and who could take over
Ask every older technician to work beyond the normal retirement age
Wait until each technician retires, then advertise the post
questions.why: Succession planning starts with a skills map: what the skills are, who holds them and who can learn them. Only then can he choose between training, recruiting and mentoring.

questions.q: Marlon finds that most of the technicians who resigned are under 30. Which step is most useful next?
o: Assume the cause is low pay and raise all technicians' salaries
Check exit interviews and pay data to learn why they leave
Stop hiring people under 30 because they tend to leave
Compare the two resignations only with last month's figures
questions.why: Two resignations show a possible pattern, not a proven cause. Marlon should find the reasons from exit interviews and other sources before choosing a response.

questions.q: If the BPO centre keeps growing by 5% a year, about how many staff will it have after two more years of growth?
questions.why: Compound growth: 800 × 1.05 = 840, then 840 × 1.05 = 882. Adding 5% of 800 twice (880) ignores growth on the first year's increase.

questions.q: Keisha wants to judge whether vacancies are rising or falling, but the monthly figures jump around. What helps most?
o: Using only the highest month of the year as the guide
Using only the most recent month as the guide to the trend
Adding all the months together into one yearly total
Averaging the latest three months, then moving it on each month
questions.why: A moving average smooths the ups and downs. For the last three months, (30 + 27 + 33) ÷ 3 = 30, compared with 27 for the three months before that, so the direction is up.

questions.q: What percentage of the 40 adverts asked for Spanish-language skills?
questions.why: 14 ÷ 40 × 100 = 35%. The base is the number of adverts (40), not the number of skills or staff.

questions.q: Which chart best compares the share of adverts that ask for each of six different skills?
o: A line graph with one line for each year
A pie chart with six thin slices of one circle
A bar chart with a bar for each skill
A single table of numbers with no chart
questions.why: Comparing amounts between groups is best shown with bars. A line graph is for change over time, and a pie chart with many slices is hard to read.

questions.q: Keisha wants to plan using the 5% yearly growth for the next five years. What is the main risk?
o: Five years is too short a period to use any past trend
Growth depends on client contracts and demand that may change
The 5% figure must be an error because growth is never steady
Staff growth cannot be measured properly using percentages
questions.why: A projection assumes the causes of the past trend will continue. A lost client contract or a new competitor could change it, so she should plan scenarios as well.

questions.q: Andrea sees staff numbers rise by 30% from December to April every year. How should she treat this?
o: As a seasonal pattern to plan for, not as business growth
As a long-term trend that proves the hotel is expanding every year
As a one-off event that can be ignored in the plan
As an error in the data that should be corrected
questions.why: A change that repeats at the same time each year is seasonal. It must be planned for every year but it does not show growth.

questions.q: How should Andrea treat the five weeks of hurricane closure when she looks at staff numbers?
o: As the start of a downward trend in staffing
As a seasonal pattern that returns every year
As proof that the hotel needs to employ more staff
As a one-off event, noted but not projected
questions.why: A hurricane that closes the hotel is a one-off event. Projecting it forward would distort the forecast, but the lesson for emergency planning should be recorded.

questions.q: What percentage of the 30 leavers gave better pay overseas as their reason, and how should she treat the finding?
o: 60%; it proves that pay is the only cause, so no other checks are needed
18%; the group is too small to use for any purpose
60%; she should ignore it, because exit interviews are not real data
60%; it is useful evidence, but she should check it against other sources
questions.why: 18 ÷ 30 × 100 = 60%. Exit interviews are useful internal data, but the group is small and self-reported, so she should confirm the trend with other sources.

questions.q: The assistant's WhatsApp poll says 80% of graduates plan to leave. What is the main reason Delroy should not rely on it?
o: It is too recent to be accurate or complete
It was collected using a phone and not on paper
It is 25 friends only, not chosen to represent graduates
It gives a percentage instead of a number of people
questions.why: A tiny sample chosen from one person's friends is not representative. A reliable source states its method and uses a large, well-chosen sample.

questions.q: The equipment seller's brochure says that half of all office jobs will vanish in five years. What should Delroy do?
o: Accept it because it is professionally printed and detailed
Check who made it, its method and whether the seller gains
Use it as the main source for the training plan
Ignore every forecast about technology from now on
questions.why: The author may profit from the claim. Delroy should check the method and compare it with independent sources before using it.

questions.q: Delroy finds that branches with more overtime have more sick leave. What is the safest conclusion?
o: The two move together; he must look for other causes
Overtime causes sick leave, so overtime should be banned at once
Sick leave causes overtime, so each branch should hire more staff
The link is chance and means nothing at all for the company
questions.why: Correlation does not prove cause. Understaffing might lead to both overtime and sickness, so he must investigate before acting.

questions.q: The firm trains some pickers to work as system operators. What is this called?
o: Reskilling
Upskilling
Succession planning
Seasonal hiring
questions.why: Reskilling means training staff for a different role. Upskilling means training them to do the same job with new skills or tools.

questions.q: The largest customer's contract may or may not be renewed. Which approach should the firm use to plan the workforce?
o: Plan only for the highest volume the customer might send
Plan only for last year's volume and review in a year
Wait until the contract decision, then start planning
Prepare plans for high-volume and low-volume cases
questions.why: When the outcome is uncertain, scenario planning prepares responses in advance and says what signals would trigger each plan.

questions.q: The strategic plan includes a refrigerated delivery service. What should the training plan do?
o: Train all staff in the same general course in the year
Leave skills planning until the new service starts
Add cold-chain and refrigeration skills to the plan
Focus training only on the automated sorting roles
questions.why: The people plan should support the strategic goals. A new service needs the matching skills, so training must be planned before the service starts.

questions.q: A hurricane closes a hotel for a month and staff hours fall sharply. An analyst projects the fall forward for the next five years. What mistake has she made?
o: She mistook a seasonal pattern for a long-term trend
She treated a one-off event as a trend
She used a moving average over too short a period
She calculated a percentage using the wrong base
questions.why: A one-off event should be noted and set aside. A projection assumes that the conditions behind a trend continue; here the cause was a single event.

questions.q: A parish has 90,000 working-age people. Its labour force (employed plus unemployed) is 63,000. What is its participation rate?
questions.why: Participation rate = labour force ÷ working-age population × 100 = 63,000 ÷ 90,000 × 100 = 70%. Check: 70% of 90,000 = 63,000.
